User flagged that issues weren't getting closed despite heavy shipping ("last issue closed 11 hours ago"). Root cause: slice PRs merge with **`Part of #NNN`**, which never auto-closes on squash-merge. That is correct for umbrellas but wrong when a PR fully satisfies a *dedicated* issue. Example: #749 (eager cascade) shipped in #755 as "Part of #749" and sat open; had to be closed by hand.

**Why:** GitHub only auto-closes on `Closes/Fixes/Resolves #NNN` in the merged PR body. "Part of" is inert. The [[feedback-pr-creation-hygiene]] rule (escape only non-issue `#NN`) is about linkage syntax; this is about the *verb*.

**How to apply:**
- A PR that fully satisfies a **dedicated** issue → `Closes #NNN` in the body (auto-closes on merge).
- **Umbrellas** (e.g. #635, #752) → `Part of #NNN`; close by hand when the last slice lands.
- Simulation-first rotation/engine slices: the primitive+sim-proof issue is DONE at that bar (production wiring is separate issues) — so `Closes` the primitive issue, don't leave it "Part of".
- Periodically sweep open `v2-build` issues vs merged PRs for completed-but-open drift; `gh issue close --comment` pointing at the delivering PR + any successor issues. Don't auto-close umbrellas or not-started/deferred issues.

The user is happy to batch **multiple loosely-related issues into one PR** to keep review cadence
flowing. Stated 2026-08-08 during wave 8.

**Why:** CodeRabbit gives one review per hour org-wide, so a wave of N single-issue PRs costs at
least N hours of review chain whatever order it runs in. The file-ownership graph caps how much can
run in *parallel*; the review slot caps how fast anything *lands*. Batching cuts the number of
cycles, and it is the only lever that moves the real bottleneck. See
[[project-v2-hot-file-contention-caps-parallelism]] for the other half of the constraint.

**How to apply:**

- Batch by **shared file surface first, topical relation second**. Two issues that both touch
  `facade.rs` belong together whether or not they are conceptually related, because splitting them
  guarantees a rebase. Two issues in the same subsystem that interact semantically (one changes
  where auth state comes from, the other what happens when restore fails) belong together because
  splitting them makes the second rework the first.
- 2–3 issues per PR is the working size. Do not build one giant PR: review quality drops, and
  CodeRabbit has a [[project-coderabbit-150-file-cap]].
- Give each issue its own commit inside the batch, and a `Closes #N` line per issue in the body.
- When adding scope to an agent already mid-build, tell it to finish the original issue coherently
  first and add the second on top — and to ship the first alone if the second turns out much larger
  than scoped. A blocked bug fix is worse than an extra review cycle.
- Still hold a batch behind a genuine blocker. Batching changes how work is grouped, never whether
  a dependency edge is respected.

Related: [[feedback-closes-vs-part-of-issue-hygiene]] (one `Closes` per finished issue),
[[feedback-keep-prs-draft-control-cr-timing.md]] (the orchestrator owns slot timing).

**Reaffirmed and strengthened 2026-08-19 (wave 11):** "I would like each of the PRs to close more
than one issue (if possible and appropriate)." Treat a single-issue PR as needing justification,
not as a default. This applies to slices already planned but **not yet opened** — re-batch them
mid-wave rather than waiting for the next wave.

Two things make re-batching easier than it looks mid-wave:

- A hot-file slot **frees the moment its PR merges**. The "one PR per wave per hot file" rule is
  about PRs in flight together, not the wave as a calendar unit. Once the `facade.rs` claimant
  merges, a later PR in the same wave can claim `facade.rs` — it just rebases.
- Combining is sometimes the *better review*, not merely the cheaper one. Two halves of one
  security protocol (server exchange + browser key custody) reviewed separately means no review
  ever sees the binding between them.

Related: [[project-worktree-branch-ref-goes-stale]] when re-batching into an existing branch.

Review target: `git diff main...HEAD`

`/simplify → 4 cleanup agents in parallel → apply the fixes`

You are improving the quality of the changed code, not hunting for bugs. Review
it for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude issues, then fix what you
find. Do not look for correctness bugs — that is what `/code-review` is for.

## Phase 0 — Gather the diff

Run `git diff @{upstream}...HEAD` (or `git diff main...HEAD` / `git diff HEAD~1`
if there's no upstream) to get the unified diff under review. If there are
uncommitted changes, or the range diff is empty, also run `git diff HEAD` and
include the working-tree changes in scope — the review often runs before the
commit. If a PR number, branch name, or file path was passed as an argument,
review that target instead. Treat this diff as the review scope.

## Phase 1 — Review (4 cleanup agents in parallel)

Launch **4 independent review agents** via the Agent tool, all in a
single message so they run concurrently. Pass each agent the diff and one of
the four angles below. Each returns its findings with `file`, `line`, a
one-line `summary`, and the concrete cost (what is duplicated, wasted, or
harder to maintain).

### Reuse

Flag new code that re-implements something the codebase
already has — Grep shared/utility modules and files adjacent to the change,
and name the existing helper to call instead.

### Simplification

Flag unnecessary complexity the diff adds: redundant or derivable state,
copy-paste with slight variation, deep nesting, dead code left behind. Name
the simpler form that does the same job.

### Efficiency

Flag wasted work the diff introduces: redundant computation or repeated I/O,
independent operations run sequentially, blocking work added to startup or
hot paths. Also flag long-lived objects built from closures or captured
environments — they keep the entire enclosing scope alive for the object's
lifetime (a memory leak when that scope holds large values); prefer a
class/struct that copies only the fields it needs. Name the cheaper
alternative.

### Altitude

Check that each change fixes the root cause at the right depth rather than
patching a symptom with a fragile bandaid. Special cases layered on shared
infrastructure are a sign the fix isn't deep enough — prefer the simpler, more
general change to the underlying mechanism over adding special cases, and name
that change.

## Phase 2 — Apply the fixes

Wait for all four agents to complete, dedup findings that point at the same
line or mechanism, and fix each remaining one directly. Skip any finding whose
fix would change intended behavior, require changes well outside the reviewed
diff, or that you judge to be a false positive — note the skip rather than
arguing with it. Finish with a brief summary of what was fixed and what was
skipped (or confirm the code was already clean).
